title: What Australia's disappearing middle means for the legal market
author: Jerome Doraisamy

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI adoption reshapes legal-service economics rather than merely improving productivity. It materially extends the synthesis with a conditional Australian-market scenario: AI-enabled cost compression and more deliberate buyer allocation could bifurcate providers into scale-first and premium firms, squeezing firms without a clear cost or premium position. Its contribution is predictive and qualitative, not evidence that this restructuring has already occurred.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI compresses routine legal production and drives buyer-side insourcing and technology-enabled delivery. It materially extends that proposition with a specific forecast for Australia: firms will bifurcate into scale-first and premium models, potentially eliminating the undifferentiated mid-market. This is presented as a prediction, not an established market outcome.

kp.k: Humphrey predicts an hourglass-shaped legal market
kp.d: Doraisamy reports Nick Humphrey’s prediction that Australia’s mid-market firms will be squeezed between proliferating specialist boutiques and larger firms pursuing acquisitions and global alliances. The article points to recent boutique launches, mergers and acquisitions as observations consistent with that forecast, while identifying talent attraction and retention as a particular mid-market challenge.
qs: The mid-market in legal services is being compressed from above by premium firms protecting complexity, and from below by scale-first firms finally having the technology to deliver volume work cheaply enough to win.

There’ll be a “proliferation” of small or boutique firms, with one or two partners; “they’ll be very specialised niche offerings, almost no back office at all, maybe a secretary and a laptop and off they go,” he suggested, and at the other end of the spectrum, “there’ll be a lot more acquisitions, a lot more global alliances” between larger law firms.
Such an “hourglass effect”, as Humphrey put it, means that mid-market practices “need to figure out how they will attract and retain their talent”.
“Mid-market firms will be fighting at all levels,” he said.

kp.k: Laird anticipates two viable firm models
kp.d: Alison Laird predicts that Australia’s legal market may bifurcate into scale-first firms handling repeatable work and premium firms protecting complex, high-value expertise, eliminating a sustainable middle position. This is a forward-looking market thesis rather than a quantified finding.
qs: For Alison Laird (pictured), the director of innovation at the College of Law, the answer may come in the form of Australia’s legal market splitting into two viable operating models: scale-first firms and premium firms.
Under such a split, the mid-market would disappear.

kp.k: Three forces are compressing the mid-market
kp.d: Laird attributes the compression to three converging forces: AI reducing routine-work production costs; more sophisticated clients and legal departments separating commodity work from complex matters and bringing work in-house; and expenses growing faster than revenue. In her account, firms without either a credible low-cost model or a premium proposition are squeezed from both directions.
qs: Firstly, she said, AI is compressing the cost of producing routine legal work, “which is putting increased pressure on the margin proposition for firms that built their book on volume without the operational infrastructure to compete on cost”.

Secondly, clients and law departments are becoming more sophisticated and becoming “far more deliberate buyers, separating commodity work from genuinely complex matters and routing them accordingly”. They’re also, she added, leveraging AI to bring more work back in-house.

Thirdly, and as a result of the above, Laird outlined, expense growth is outpacing revenue growth across most of the market, “which means firms that lack a clear cost or premium story are being squeezed from both ends at the same time”.

kp.k: AI efficiencies are becoming operational expectations
kp.d: Laird asserts that the change is accelerating because AI has progressed from pilots to embedded production use by 2026. She says clients now expect operational efficiency gains to appear in firms’ prices and services, although the article supplies no study, sample or quantitative measure supporting this market-wide claim.
qs: “I think the reason it’s accelerating now rather than five years ago is that AI has moved from pilot to production, and now, in many cases, is embedded as ‘the way we do things around here’. Efficiency gains that were theoretical in 2023 are operational in 2026, and clients expect to see them reflected in price and service,” she said.

kp.k: Scale-first providers can undercut traditional competitors
kp.d: The article characterises technology as enabling scale-first firms to deliver high-volume legal work more cheaply, while premium firms retain genuinely complex matters. This cost-capability shift is presented as the mechanism by which providers at the lower end can take work from undifferentiated mid-market firms.
qs: In short: Australia’s mid-market for legal services is getting squeezed from the large end of town, which is moving to protect complexity, and then also from below, with scale-first firms now having the technological capability to deliver volume work in a cheaper fashion, allowing them to muscle out competitors.

kp.k: Compression threatens work, margins and talent
kp.d: Laird says the effects may compound across work allocation, margins and talent: clients route work to firms or ALSPs with clearer propositions, weak differentiation undermines rate integrity and annual increases, and strong performers leave firms lacking direction. She frames shrinking margins as a structural signal rather than a temporary pricing issue.
qs: “Work is drifting towards firms or ALSPs with clearer value propositions. Margin is eroding because neither the volume nor the premium story is credible enough to justify rate integrity or annual rate rises. And talent (often the most underappreciated casualty) suffers as a result, with strong performers looking to work somewhere with a clear direction.
This leads, Laird said, to a cycle in which “without the talent to deliver the work, you won’t get the work to attract the talent”.
“If firms treat shrinking margins as a temporary pricing problem rather than a structural signal, then that is cause for concern,” she said.

kp.k: Scale-first firms require redesigned operating infrastructure
kp.d: Laird recommends that firms choosing a scale-first model invest in process infrastructure, legal technology and pricing systems for confidently scoping and delivering repeatable work. The model requires accepting lower margins per matter in return for greater throughput and restructuring the firm around those economics.
qs: According to Laird, “if you’re building towards a scale-first model, you should be investing in process infrastructure, legal technology, and pricing systems that let you scope and deliver repeatable work with confidence”.
“With that model, you accept lower margin per matter in exchange for higher throughput, and you restructure around those economics,” she said.

kp.k: Premium firms need depth and client selectivity
kp.d: For a premium model, Laird recommends concentrating on genuine depth in defined practice areas, protecting rates and expertise value, narrowing the client base and abandoning work that does not fit. She says this strategic choice should immediately affect client targeting, pricing priorities and which work the firm stops performing.
qs: If firms wish to focus on building towards, or sustaining, a premium model, then they will have to double down on genuine depth in defined practice areas, she suggested.

“This means protecting your rate integrity (and expertise ‘value’), and get far more selective about your client base. It’s time to get rid of the long ‘tail’ and focus on the ‘20’ of the 80/20 rule,” Laird said.
What will ultimately then change, “immediately and concretely”, Laird said, is which clients a firm pursues, the work a firm aggressively prices for, and the work it stops doing entirely.

“I haven’t yet come across a firm that relishes saying ‘no’ to an existing revenue stream. But continuing to service work that doesn’t fit either model will only delay the reckoning I think is coming, and potentially weakens the position you’re trying to build,” she said.

kp.k: Clients may impose firms’ strategic positioning
kp.d: Laird warns that firms may lose the opportunity to select their own model because clients can silently reroute matter types, including to panel ALSPs. She treats disappearing pitch invitations as an early signal that may precede visible revenue deterioration, making revenue data a lagging indicator of market positioning.
qs: This said, it is entirely possible, Laird mused, that the market will make such decisions for firms, rather than the other way around.
“One of the clearest signals is when clients stop inviting you to pitch for particular matter types without ever formally telling you why. The work just routes elsewhere,” she said.
“By the time that pattern is visible in revenue data, the market has already formed a view of where you sit. Think about how many clients now have ALSPs on their panels.”

kp.k: Strategic candour is preferable to inertial drift
kp.d: Laird says proactive firms explicitly decide what kind of firm they intend to become rather than treating the issue as generic transformation. She argues that passive drift is still a strategic decision, but one determined by existing clients and capabilities, and predicts only a limited window for deliberate choice.
qs: They’ve not, she said, dressed it up as a transformation, but have called it what it is: “a choice about what kind of firm we’re going to be”.

“More common is a quiet drift towards whichever operating model the firm’s existing client mix and capability base already imply – which is still a decision, just one that gets made by inertia rather than intention,” Laird said.
“I think there is a limited window here for firms to have some tough conversations and make that decision for themselves, before the market does.”

kp.k: Accounting provides an analogy for legal bifurcation
kp.d: As cross-domain analogy rather than direct legal-market evidence, Laird says accounting is further along: the Big Four moved away from small- and mid-size audit work while expanding premium advisory services and technology-enabled volume compliance. She predicts law will follow a similar path more quickly.
qs: The accounting profession, she said, is a step ahead, with the big four firms having pivoted away from the small- to mid-size audit market, while building out their more profitable advisory capabilities at the premium end, with technology-enabled compliance platforms at the volume end.
“Nobody called it bifurcation at the time. It just happened. I think law is heading to the same place, just faster, and with perhaps less excuse for being surprised by it!” Laird said.

kp.k: AI exposes systematisable portions of legal work
kp.d: Laird argues that lawyers’ cultural tendency to regard every matter as unique has delayed market restructuring, even though significant portions of legal work can be systematised. In her account, AI is now exposing that mismatch and accelerating compression more rapidly than in other professional services.
qs: What’s different in the legal profession, Laird observed, is the pace of compression and the cultural resistance to acknowledging it.
“Generally, lawyers are trained to see every matter as unique – and some elements are – but significant portions of legal work are ‘systematisable’,” she said.
“That belief in uniqueness has already sustained the middle longer than market logic ever warranted. And now AI is exposing it.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Laird argues that AI-driven cost compression and more deliberate buying are squeezing mid-market firms, potentially splitting Australia's legal market into scale-first and premium operating models.
pts.d: Alison Laird, director of innovation at the College of Law, says AI reduces the cost of routine legal production, undermining volume practices without the infrastructure to compete on cost. Buyers increasingly separate commodity work from complex matters and use AI to bring work in-house. Together with expense growth exceeding revenue growth, these forces could eliminate the undifferentiated mid-market. Doraisamy frames this as pressure from premium firms protecting complex work and scale-first firms delivering volume work more cheaply. Laird identifies potential compounding losses of work, margins and talent, with work moving to firms or ALSPs offering clearer value propositions. This is a prediction about market positioning and operating models, not a claim that AI necessarily eliminates every firm currently classified as mid-sized. Humphrey's related 'hourglass effect' describes market polarisation here, not a firm's internal staffing structure.

pts.k: Laird predicts that firms must choose between technology-enabled throughput and differentiated premium expertise, changing their pricing, client selection and work mix.
pts.d: For a scale-first model, Laird recommends process infrastructure, legal technology and pricing systems supporting repeatable work, with lower margins per matter offset by higher throughput. For a premium model, she recommends genuine practice-area depth, protection of rates and more selective client acceptance. Firms that avoid choosing may instead have their positioning determined by buyers routing work elsewhere. She also argues that AI exposes how much legal work can be systematised, challenging the profession's belief in matter uniqueness.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The argument rests on interviewed practitioners' assessments, illustrative firm developments and an accounting-sector analogy, rather than quantified AI or market evidence.
pts.d: Laird offers professional observations about AI deployment, buyer behaviour, economics and firm strategy; the article supplies no datasets, measured cost reductions, adoption rates or benchmarks establishing those claims. Doraisamy supports Humphrey's broader market-polarisation forecast with boutique launches, national firms acquiring smaller practices, and the named mergers of Herbert Smith Freehills and Kramer Levin, Ashurst and Perkins Coie, and Allen & Overy and Shearman Sterling. He notes the King & Wood Mallesons decoupling as a countertrend. These are illustrations of market restructuring, not measurements of AI's causal contribution. Laird further draws an analogy with accounting: she says the Big Four shifted away from small- to mid-size audits while developing premium advisory and technology-enabled volume compliance. That comparison concerns their accounting-sector strategy, not evidence about their entry into legal services.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Laird presents the squeeze as already occurring in March 2026 and accelerating as AI moves into production, but gives no deadline for the mid-market's predicted disappearance.
pts.d: Laird explicitly contrasts theoretical efficiency gains in 2023 with operational gains in 2026, qualifying embedded adoption as occurring 'in many cases'. Clients are said already to expect benefits in price and service. The potential loss of work, margin and talent is conditional rather than universal: Laird says all three could compound, especially where firms lack a credible cost or premium proposition. The strategic response should change client targeting and work selection immediately. Her forecast gives firms a limited but unspecified window to choose a model; disappearance of the middle remains a possible outcome rather than a dated certainty.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are undifferentiated mid-market firms, scale-first and premium competitors, ALSPs, corporate buyers and mobile legal talent.
pts.d: Mid-market firms face lost instructions, eroding pricing power and difficulty retaining strong performers. Scale-first firms can compete for repeatable work through lower-cost delivery; premium firms can concentrate on genuinely complex matters and expertise-based pricing. ALSPs are identified as alternative destinations for client work, not as software vendors. Corporate legal departments become more deliberate purchasers and use AI to insource work. Humphrey separately describes talent competition from high-paying top-end firms, private-equity-backed firms offering equity, and independent niche boutiques. The source does not quantify employment losses or claim that junior lawyers specifically will be displaced.
